course.title: Gastric cancer
course.html:
EpidemiologyRisk factors
- 4th common cause of cancer related death
- More common in males
- Black race
- Individuals with low socio-economic status
- In developing countries
- In Asia (Japan, Korea)		1. H. pylori infection !!!
2. Smoking
3. Excessive salt ingestion; salt/smoke preserved food
4. Diet low on fresh fruits and vegetables
5. Hereditary GC or HNPCC (hereditary non polyposic colon cancer
syndrome) (Lynch II; gastric and colic cancer)
6. Predisposing gastric disease
→ Giant hypertrophic gastropathy (Menetrier’s)
(inner lining of stomach forms huge folds, due to excessive overgrowth of mucous)
→ Adenomatous polyps (≥ 2cm) (present atypia)
→ Chronic atrophic gastritis
→ Partial gastrectomy for peptic ulcer (not done any longer; 20-30 y. ago)
→ Intestinal metaplasia (often in smoking, H. pylori)

Carciogenesis

  • 1. Intestinal metaplasia - chronic inflamed gastric mucosa morphing into intestinal mucosa
  • 2. Dysplasia - structural degeneration in 3 degrees (light, medium, severe)
    • Light dysplasia may not require surgical treatment
    • Severe dysplasia = carcinoma in situ; requires endoscopic mucosal excision or surgical gastric resection
  • 3. Invasive carcinoma = final step

Pathology

External aspect- Advanced tumors are visible and palpable on surface of stomach
→ firm, infiltrated, white/ grey colored
Endogastric
aspect
(gastroscopy)		- Can differentiate between 2 types of GC
a) Early gastric CA
b) Advanced gastric CA
a)Early gastric CA
b)Advanced gastric CA

EARLY GASTRIC CA (EGC)

  • Local adenoCA limited to gastric mucosa or submucosa
  • With or without lymph node metastasis (N0, N1)
  • Best prognosis with 5-year survival rate >90%
  • Diagnosis in early stage of disease is established by endoscopy only (active mass screening !)

Paris endoscopic classification of EGC

Type 0-I- Protrusive, exophytic
- Rough, protrusive, malignant small polyp
Type 0-IIType 0-IIa- Slightly elevated (up to 5mm above the surrounding mucosa)
Type 0-IIb- Flat, discolored mucosa
Type 0-IIc- Slightly depressed
Type 0-III- Superficial ulceration

ADVANCED GASTRIC CA (AGC)

  • Extension of malignant infiltration beyond submucosa

Borrmann classification system

Type I- Protrusive, proliferative
Type II- Ulcerative, with elevated uneven margins
Type III- Ulcerative-infiltrative uncertainly contoured tumor with deep central crater
Type IV- Extensive infiltrating with important thickening of the gastric wall

Histology

  • Majority → adenocarcinomas (> 90%)
  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumors = GISTs
  • Non-Hodgkin gastric lymphomas
  • Neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid, gastrinoma)

Shah’s classification (2010) + Lauren’s classification (1963) for adenocarcinoma subtypes

  • important for gastric location, prognosis and carcinogenetic mechanism
Intestinal type- Body or antrum (non-diffuse, non-proximal)
- Most common variant
- Chronic inflammation → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → invasive CA
Risk factors
- Helicobacter pylori infection
- Cigarette smoking
- High salt intake
- Alcohol consumption
GEJ and cardia
(proximal !)		- Infection with H. pylori seems to have protective effect (resulted severe atrophic
gastritis and aclorhydria, diminishes risk of gastroesophageal reflux)
- Prognosis is worse and resectability rates are lower
Diffuse type- Triggered by gene (E-cadherin) mutation
- Malignant cells progressively + diffusely infiltrate gastric wall → extended thickening
of entire stomach → rigid tube
- Diffuse, total infiltration of entire stomach = linitis plastica/ gastric schirus
- Tends to appear in younger patients
- Has the worst prognosis
- No precursor lesion has been identified

Diagnosis of gastric cancer

  • Often no specific clinical symptoms
Unspecific signs and symptoms (early)Alarm symptoms (advanced)
- Epigastric discomfort
- Flatulence
- Discrete swollen belly after meals (postprandial
meteorism)
- Early satiation
- Malaise		- Dysphagia
- Upper GI hemorrhage
- Fatigue
- Anemia
- Weight loss
- Selective anorexia (for meat, bread)
- Epigastric palpable tumor

Juxtaorifcially situated tumors (eso-gastric junction or pyloric) can manifest earlier

  • Early dysphagia/ GERD (heartburn, regurgitation) → eso-gastric tumors
  • Delayed gastric emptying by malignant gastric outlet obstruction/ stenosis, fullness, bloating, vomiting,

dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, weight loss, emaciation → distal antro pyloric tumor

  • Anemic syndrome (common finding in malignant GI tumors)
  • Upper GI bleeding is occult → clinically undetectable, but persistent
  • Chronic iron deficiency anemia → headache, physical and psychic asthenia, decreased productivity, pallor of skin and mucosa, weakness, fatigue
  • doing an hemoccult test, if positive → endoscopic evaluation (chance of early diagnosis !)

Upper GI bleeding

  • Dramatic, fulminant, immediately life-threatening bleedings can occur (rare)
  • Moderate bleedings – hematemesis and/or melena

Abnormal nutritional status

  • weight loss despite initial normal appetite
  • anorexia (first selective, later general)
  • cachexia (end stage)
  • best reflected by albumin

In very advanced stages (always indicating irresectability !)

  • Jaundice → liver metastasis or CBD compression
  • Irregular liver margins → large liver metastasis
  • Intense and persisting epigastric pain → invasion of celiac plexus or pancreas
  • Increase in abdominal volume → ascites → peritoneal carcinomatosis
  • Virchow nodule (left supraclavicular or laterocervical)
  • Krunkenberg tumor → ovarian metastasis (CA 125)
  • Sister Mary Joseph nodule → umbilical metastasis
  • Blumer shelf → mobile tumor detected in Douglas pouch during DRE

Paraclinical diagnosis

1. Barium exam- Double contrast, segmental rigidity of infiltrated area, lacunar image
(not used anymore)
2. Gastro-
duodenofibroscopy
(Gastroscopy)		2. Gastro-= main examination
→ direct visualization and possibility of biopsy (only way of pre-OP diagnosis !)
→ negative biopsy doesn’t rule out existence of cancer !
- Red, irregular tumor or ulceration, grey/necrotic areas, quick to bleed when touched
- Malignant ulcerations may be mistaken for benign ulcers
- If biopsy is negative → endoscopic re-exam in 6-8 weeks or whenever suspicion for
malignancy arises
- Brushing cytology exam (gentle brushing of lesion) may detect malignant cells where
biopsies failed to confirm malignancy
Modern endoscopic techniques to detect very small, superficial lesions
- Magnifying endoscopy
- Narrow band imaging
- Chromoendoscopy
duodenofibroscopy
(Gastroscopy)
3. Endoscopic US= most accurate examination in terms of local tumor extension (T)
4. Percutaneous US- First intent to see lymph nodes (N stage), ascites or liver (M stage; especially with CEUS)
- They offer valuable information about local tumor extension and distant metastasis of
GC (liver, lung)
→ Perfect for T, N, M staging!
5. CT
6. MRI
7. PET
8. Staging laparoscopy8. Staging laparoscopy- Only in selected cases; not routinely
- May detect small (mm) lesions, which cannot be detected by any other exam
(peritoneal carcinomatosis = M1, disseminated disease – stage IV ! → operation is not
indicated because it does not offer survival benefits)
9. Tumor markers→ CEA, CA 19.9, CA 72.4, CA 50
- Lacking specificity → prognostic factors
- Increased mostly in advanced stages
- Play role in appreciating accuracy of surgical resection (should drop post-OP)
- May rise during post-OP follow-up → metastasis, local recurrence
10. Circulating RNA=circRNA→ may detect early GC (EGC) with sensitivity of 77.5 %

Evolution and prognosis

  • Untreated - 1 year survival
  • Proper treatment (gastric Ro resection) - 20% survive 5 years
  • EGC, when treated → survival rate at 5 years > 90% (importance of early diagnosis !)
  • GC at body or fundus are frequently found too late (lacking symptoms)
  • Distal (antro pyloric) tumors have highest respectability rates and best prognosis

Complications (similar to ulcers)

  • Hemorrhage
  • Stenosis
  • Perforation
  • Invasion of neighboring viscera, metastasis
  • Blumer's shelf (metastasis in Douglas pouch) or Krukenberg tumors

Treatment

  • Based on T and N staging
  • Radical, complete (R0) resection
EARLY GCADVANCED GC
- Tis, T1a, T1b → endoscopic resection
- Preserving morphologic and functional integrity
of abdominal wall and stomach !
- Only in intestinal types (not diffuse !)
- Confined to mucosa/ submucosa (Tis, T1a/b)
- Without lymph node involvement (N0)
- Eradication of H. pylori is mandatory ! to
prevent metachronous gastric carcinoma
a) Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR)
- Confined to mucosa
- Well differentiated, elevated, < 20mm
- Well diff., depressed, < 10mm, no ulcer
- Larger lesions cannot always be totally resected
(risk of recurrence – R1 resection!)
b) Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD)
- Mucosal: well differentiated, > 20 mm, no ulcer
- Mucosal: well differentiated, ≤ 30 mm, with ulcer
- Submucosal: well differentiated, ≤ 30 mm
- Allows larger/ deeper resection
c) Endoscopic full thickness resection (EFTR)
- Allows biopsy of small tumor with all layers
around tumor (“full thickness”)
→ Resulted gastric wall defect is closed with clips		≥ T2 tumor or N1
1. Neoadjuvant therapy → N1
2. Surgery → R0 resection
3. Adjuvant therapy
BUT NOT SURGERY FIRST!
- The only treatment for actual healing is R0
radical surgical resection (margins 5-6 cm from tumor)
→ Removal of stomach along with regional lymph
nodes → no tumor cells left behind !
a) Wedge resection
→ Only in well selected early submucosal gastric CA
→ Appropriate for GISTs
b) Subtotal gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
→ In distal (antropyloric) gastric tumors
- Resection includes duodenum (3 cm distal from
pylorus), pylorus and distal 3/4 or 4/5 of stomach
+ gastro-duodenal / gastro-jejuno-anastomosis
c) Total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
→ Tumors located proximal (body, fundus)
- Entire stomach + 3-5cm of distal esophagus
+ ROUX en Y eso-jejunostomy
Both gastrectomies require omentectomy (large and
small) and regional (D2) lymphadenectomy		≥ T2 tumor or N1

* Omentectomy removes perigastric lymph nodes (groups 1, 3, 4, 5, 6)

Extension of lymphadenectomy (stations 7-12) = D2 lymphadenectomy

Reconstruction

After subtotal gastrectomyAfter total gastrectomy
1. Duodenal stump
(termino-terminal gastro-duodenostomy –Bilroth I )
2. First jejunal loop
(termino-lateral gastro-jejunostomy – Bilroth II )
3. Roux-en-Y jejunal loop
(termino-lateral Roux en Y gastro-jejunostomy)		- Duodenal stump is closed
1. Roux-en Y jejunal loop
(termino-lateral eso-jejunostomy)
2. Bilroth II with Braun anastomosis
(in cases in which, due to anatomy/vascular “1.” can’t be
prepared)
  • Nowadays the laparoscopic approach for all procedures in preferred

Complication and palliative therapy

  • 1. Hemorrhage → endoscopy → if not working, emergency gastrectomy, vascular pedicles ligation
  • 2. Perforation → spilling gastric content (with tumor cells !) into peritoneal cavity → diffuse “carcinomatous seeding”
  • resection is only option (this time for palliation only)
  • 3. Stenosis/ gastric outlet obstruction → endoprosthesis/ endoscopic stenting → if it fails, open gastro-enterostomy
  • local extended tumor (unresectable) → latero-lateral gastro-jejunostomy
  • for proximal stenoses (GEJ) producing impressive cachexia → endoprosthesis or gastrectomy/ jejunostomy

course.title: Benign gastric disorders
course.html:
Peptic ulcer

= localized histopathological lesion → “lack of substance” involving mucosa, muscularis mucosae, submucosa;

sometimes affects also muscularis layer, progressing through serosa

  • Both locations (stomach and duodenum)
  • Can be perforated or not
  • Duodenum – young males
  • Stomach – older age, low social status

Gastric ulcers

  • Imbalance between defending mechanism of mucosa and

hydrochloric acid aggression

Mucosal defense factorsMucosal aggression factors
- Intense cellular turn-over
- Secretion of mucus
- Secretion of HCO3 in duodenum
- Adequate blood supply		- H. pylori infection (inflammation)
- NSAIDs (lowers PG´s)
- Acid hypersecretion (gastrinoma, Zollinger-Ellison)
- Duodeno-gastric reflux (bile)
- Gastric stasis
- Alcohol and smoking = irritants → decreased production
of PG’s and gastric mucosal ischemia

Duodenal ulcers

  • Acid hypersecretion
  • H. Pylori, NSAIDs, motility disorders of the stomach (rapid evacuation → high amounts of acid), smoking

Clinical features and diagnosis

  • Epigastric or hypochondriac pain (towards left = gastric; towards right = duodenal) (gastric ulcer → aggravated by food, worse during day; duodenal ulcer → relieved by food, worse during night)
  • “Painful hunger”, relieve by milk
  • Nausea, vomiting, fullness, weight loss/ gain
  • Physical exam – nonspecific; epigastric dullness at palpation
  • Lab test – nonspecific; BUT H. pylori breath and fecal test!!!
  • Gold standard → Endoscopy with biopsy (from lesion and surrounding tissue to rule out CA and to check for H. pylori)
  • Radiology with hydrosoluble contrast - “Haudek niche” is characteristic for ulcers

Johnson classification of ulcers (related to ulcer location)

Type I= single ulcer, localized at gastric angle
Type II= gastric and duodenal ulcer
Type III= consists in single lesion located pre-pyloric
Type IV= located high on lesser curvature, right under cardia
Type V= caused by use of NSAIDs; located anywhere on stomach
Type I + IV = typical gastric ulcers, are not caused by hyperacidity
Type II + III = manifest more as a duodenal ulcer, hyperacidity
  • Acute ulcers: < 1 cm, fine wedges
  • Chronic ulcers: > 2 cm, fibrous, infiltrated wedges

Treatment (uncomplicated ulcer)

  • Gastric antisecretory drugs (PPIs, histamine antagonists)
  • Antacid
  • Gastro-duodenal mucosal protection (magnesium, aluminum salts, prostaglandins)
  • H. pylori eradication (Maastricht therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin)
  • Surgery only in cases of life-threatening complications or no responds to drug therapy

Complications

  • Perforation
  • Hemorrhage (more often)
  • Gastric outlet obstruction (due to chronic evolution)

Perforated peptic ulcer

  • Due to progression of lesion (ulcer) through entire gastric/ duodenal wall
  • Followed by discharge of gastric content into peritoneum → chemical peritonitis → bacterial peritonitis

(typically localized)

  • Mainly anterior wall ulcers
  • Especially males, thirties or forties
Free perforation= classical form, frequent
- With generalized secondary peritonitis
Covered perforation- Clinical manifestation varying
- Frust form - perforation diameter is small and it is covered from beginning by
peritoneal reaction
- Or localized peritonitis (peritoneal abscesses)
Penetration- Represents erosion towards and through neighboring organs
- When penetration happens into cavitary organ → fistula (gastro-colic, duodeno-colic)

Symptoms

  • 20% present with perforation without prior manifestations
  • Aggravation factors found in 50%: smoking, NSADs, aspirin, stress
Pain- First epigastric, can radiate towards shoulders (diaphragmatic irritation), then to right flank
and at the end generalized
- Either progressive or sudden-severe
Vomiting- Not mandatory
- Can be due to pain
- Can present with hematemesis
- Abundant in paralytic ileus
Shock state- Peritoneal irritation → vago-vagal reflexes → bradycardia, hypotension, pallor, sweating
- Hypovolemic or toxic due to bacterial peritonitis
Peritonitis- “wodden abdomen” = involuntary guarding
- Rectal/ vaginal exam is very painful → irritation of Douglas pouch
- Later abd. distension disappears
- Superficial respiration
- Paralytic ileus
Disappearance
of hepatic
dullness		- Result of gas accumulation and phrenic irritation, but they are not constant
Respiratory
impairment
Acute phase0-2 h
Chemical peritonitis → pain, abdominal contracture
Intermittent stage2-12 h
Bacterial peritonitis onset → clinical eased
Late phase> 12 h
Bacterial peritonitis – Toxico-septic shock
→ Clinical signs dominated by massive abdominal distension

Lab

  • Leukocytosis
  • ↑ serum and urine amylase

Imaging

  • Plain abdominal X-ray → pneumoperitoneum (free gas under diaphragm; mainly right)
  • Barium swallowing is forbidden
  • CT
  • Upper endoscopy is totally forbidden → gas insufflation will increase pneumoperitoneum and will accelerate spill of

gastric content; in cases with covered perforation, gas insufflation could separate adventia that block ulcer

Positive diagnosis

  • Pat. history and pneumoperitoneum
  • 3 cardinal signs of perforated peptic ulcer = acute pain, abdominal rigidity, history of ulcer

DD

  • Ulcer penetration
  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Acute cholecystitis
  • Renal colic
  • Intestinal infarction
  • Inferior MI
  • Basal pneumonitis
  • Zona zoster

Treatment

  • 1. Resting in bed
  • 2. Installation of naso-gastric tube and active aspiration of content
  • 3. Establishment of intravenous ways – at least two, administration of crystalloid solution
  • 4. Inject PPI´s iv (alternative anti-H2)
  • 5. Broad spectrum antibiotics iv
  • 6. Administration of iv short acting time antalgic (petidine)
  • 7. Urgent transport in surgical emergency unit

A. Non-surgical treatment = always 2nd choice

  • Taylor therapy
    • Nihil per os (no oral intake!)
    • Nasogastric aspiration
    • Hydroelectrolytic rebalance
    • iv PPI´s
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics
    • H. pylori eradication therapy (involves initial antibiotic regimen for 2 weeks and inhibition of gastric acid for 4)
Indications for conservative treatmentContraindications for conservative treatment
1. absolutely certainty that perforation is blocked
and no signs of generalized peritonitis
2. perforation occurred days ago and status of
patient is stable
3. presence of two rules above + patient could be
evaluated clinico-radiological every time needed
4. no surgical facility available (ships, oil rigs,
isolated sites)
5. elderly patients with no signs of peritonitis,
but with high anesthetic and surgical risk		1. Positive signs of peritonitis
2. Contrast spill at radiology
3. Hemodynamic instability, state of shock
4. Elderly, but with low operatory risk
5. Impossibility to follow course of patient
6. Failure of conservative treatment after 12-24h

B. Surgical treatment

= optimal method with best results → 1st choice!

  • 1. Suture of ulcer with patch of great omentum and abundant peritoneal wash out
  • 2. Gastric resection (definitive treatment)
  • Usually not preferred, only in …
    • a) Perforation is accompanied by GI hemorrhage
    • b) Perforation is accompanied by stenosis
    • c) There is a suspicion of a malignant gastric lesion
    • d) Suture perforation leading to stenosis
    • e) Perforation occurs after a correctly and appropriate treatment

Follow-up

  • i.v. PPI (continuous perfusion or bolus administration)
  • Drainage tube ex usually in first 3 days (when they don’t leak any liquids)
  • PPI treatment for at least 4 w
  • Control gastroscopy will assess healing of ulcer
  • If H. pylori infection present → eradication is mandatory

Peptic ulcer hemorrhage

  • 70% of upper GI hemorrhage
  • Can become life threatening
  • Bleeding from mucosal/ submucosal vessel mainly acute ulcers → usually spontaneous hemostasis
  • Bleeding of major vessel (pyloric/ gastroduodenal/ left gastric/ splenic artery) mainly chronic ulcers
    • requires endoscopic or surgical hemostasis

Clinically

  • Pallor, restlessness, faintness
  • Thirst and cold
  • Tachycardia, hypotension
  • Externalization of bleeding is by hematemesis and melena
  • Upper GI endoscopy = first indicated maneuver (diagnostic and therapeutic)
Forrest classification
Class IIaPressure (jet arterial) bleeding →emergency surgery
IbSlow continuous bleeding – endoscopic hemostasis
Class IIIIaStopped bleeding with clot adherent to crater → intensive drug ulcer therapy
IIbStopped bleeding, visible vessel in crater → emergency surgery
high risk of re-bleeding
IIcBleeding stopped, black crater of lesion → standard drug treatment
Class IINo signs of bleeding ulcer, it appears only in history → standard drug treatment

DD

  • Epistaxis, hemoptysis
  • Hemangiomas
  • Vascular abnormalities, atherosclerosis
  • Thrombocytopenia, Hemophilia, Anticoagulant therapy
  • Ruptured esophageal varices
  • Mucosal erosions
  • Pharyngeal, esophageal or gastric tumors
  • Mallory Weiss syndrome

Treatment

1. Resuscitation- i.v. line for administration of crystalloids/ colloids and possible transfusions
- Nasogastric suction tube
- Uretrovesical catheter to monitor urine output and water balance
- Check of blood group and Rh, Hb, Hct (cross-matching)
2. Hemostasis- First choice is endoscopic
1. Submucosal injection of vasoconstrictor and sclerosing substances
2. Thermoregulation
3. Application of clips to bleeding vessels
3. Surgical
treatment		- Type Ia, IIa
- Less common due to good endoscopic treatment
Clinical features that indicate surgeryEndoscopic features that indicate surgery
1. Age > 60 years
2. Long history of ulcer
3. Frequent relapse on full treatment
4. Continued melena or hematemesis
5. > 4 units of blood transfusion required
during resuscitation		1. Active bleeding (Forrest Ia)
2. Visible vessel (Forrest IIb)
3. Continued bleeding despite correct endoscopic ther.
4. Relapse after endoscopic treatment
5. Torrential bleeding that make impossible entification
of the lesion

Gastroduodenal outflow obstruction

= pyloric stenosis or other parts of stomach (e.g., mediogastric stenosis)

  • Result of long evolution of duodenal and pre-pyloric ulcers → development of fibrosis and wall deformation
  • Gastric stasis > 200ml after fasting and pediatric endoscope cannot pass through narrowed area
  • Stomach is compensating by dilatation and hypertrophy of muscularis → failure of mechanism = dilation and vomiting

Clinical

  • Stenic phase = first
    • stomach fighting stenosis
    • few symptoms
  • Atonic phase → stomach evacuation failure syndrome
    • main symptoms occur
    • vomiting with gastric juice, food ingested 1 or 2 days before and always free from bile
    • fullness in left hypochondrium
    • loss of weight
    • dehydration
    • constipation
    • weakness
    • pain +/-
    • late stage: dilatation of stomach, severe dehydration, complete digestive intolerance to food/ water, shock
  • Vomiting = outstanding symptom
  • first vomiting is accompanied by nausea, then becomes effortless, explosive without any premonitory signs
  • Humoral-metabolic syndrome = Darrow syndrome (hypoNa, hypoK, hypoCl with metabolic alkalosis and

paradoxical aciduria)

Kuessmaul sign
Clapotage sign

Diagnosis

  • Endoscopy: dilated stomach, chronic ulcer and stenosis, usually in pyloric region, insurmountable by pediatric endoscope
  • Barium meal
  • stenic phase: hyperkinesis of antrum, weak duodenal passage, barium seen as snowflakes due to high amount of

gastric juice

  • atone phase: dilated stomach appears dropped in pelvic area looking as “in sink”

DD: gastric CA, benign tumors, foreign bodies, compression from outside, corrosive stricture, achalasia

Treatment

  • 1) Rebalance of hydration and acid base status
    • a) Insert nasogastric tube for aspiration
    • b) At least two venous access point, Saline solution with supplement of ions if necessary, will be administrated,

under control of ASTRUP parameters (Na, K)

  • c) Protein solution (amino acids, albumin) in hypoproteinemia
  • d) If anemia, blood transfusion
  • surgery can be done only when the patient is well balanced
  • high risk of cardiac arrest (electrolyte imbalance) + anastomotic fistula (hypoproteinemia)
  • 2) Relieve of obstruction
    • a) Endoscopic dilation (high surgery risk)
    • b) Gastric resection with gastro-duodenal (Pean or Billroth I) or gastro-jejunal (Hoffmeister-Finsterer or Billroth II)

a. distal gastro-duodenal resection (Pean-Bilroth I); b. termino-terminal gastro-duodenostomy;

c. termino-lateral Reichel-Polya gastro-jejunostomy; d. termino-lateral Hoffmeister-Finsterer gastro-jejunostomy

Post-gastrectomy complications

  • 1. Dumping syndrome
Early Dumping syndrome→ 15 min after ingestion of osmotic meals (sugars)
- Anxiety, weakness, tachycardia, diaphoresis, and, frequently,
palpitations (i.e., vasomotor symptoms)
- Extreme weakness, crampy abdominal pain, diarrhea
- Pathophysiology: sudden discharge of hyperosmotic meal into the
intestine – movement of liquid from intravascular into intralumenal
- The release of several hormonal substances, including serotonin,
neurotensin, histamine, glucagon, VIP, kinins
Treatment
- Fractionated, multiple meals per day
- Avoidance of hyperosmotic food
- Liquids 30 minutes before or after the meal
- Somatostatin usage
- Surgical conversion to Roux-en-Y gastro-jejunal anastomosis
Late Dumping syndrome→ 3h after meals
- Anxiety, diaphoresis, tachycardia, palpitations, weakness, fatigue, and a
desire to lie down
- No diarrhea or borborygmi
- Serum glucose levels are increasing rapidly – insulin secretion overcome
needs – hypoglycemia
Treatment
- Small snacks after the meal
- Acarbose (α-glycosidase hydrolase inhibitor)
  • 2. Post-vagotomy diarrhea
  • Enhanced intestinal motility (vagal denervation), rapid gastric emptying, bile malabsorption and bacterial overgrowth
  • Diarrhea that is explosive in onset, is not related to meals, and occurs without warning
  • Fuid intake is restricted
  • Antidiarrheal/antimotility agents such as codeine, diphenoxylate hydrochloride, or loperamide
  • 3. Blind loop syndrome
  • Bacterial overgrowth in the limb of intestine that is excluded from the ﬂﬂow of chyme
  • Diarrhea, weight loss, and weakness, and they are often anemic (megaloblastic – lack of vitaminB12)
  • 4. Afferent loop obstruction

= a kink in the afferent limb adjacent to the anastomosis

  • Severe cramping abdominal pain that occurs immediately after the ingestion of a meal followed by nausea and vomiting of a dark brown, bitter-tasting material
  • 5. Alkaline reflux gastritis
  • Gastro-duodenal or gastro-jejunal anastomosis (Billroth 1 and 2)
  • Weakness, weight loss, persistent nausea, and epigastric abdominal pain that often radiates to Back
  • Edematous, bile-stained gastric epithelium that is atrophic and erythematous
  • Conversion Roux-en-Y
  • 6. Marginal and recurrent ulcer disease
  • Ulcer on the jejunal of the anastomosis
  • Abdominal pain during eating as well as nausea and vomiting
  • Stop tobacco use and initiation of a PPI
  • Insufficient gastric resection/ vagotomy
  • Hyperparathyroidism
  • Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • 7. Metabolic disturbances
  • Vitamin B12 or folate deﬁﬁciency – megaloblastic anemia (20%)
  • Iron deficiency (low absorption or chronic loss) – microcytic anemia (50%)
  • Altered bowel function is common (25%)

The stomach and the duodenum Benign gastric and duodenal disorders

Marius Stanca

The benign gastric and duodenal pathology consist in majority of cases of peptic ulcer and its complications, but includes, also, non-malignant tumors, diverticula, gastric volvulus, erosions, and foreign bodies.

Peptic ulcer

Definition: peptic ulcer PU (it includes both locations, the stomach and the duodenum) consists in a localised histopathological lesions, figured by a “lack of substance” involving the mucosa, muscularis mucasae, submucosa and, sometimes affects the muscularis layer, progressing through the serosa, which can be perforated or not. Peptic ulcer is a different pathology by the erosions and ulcerations, whom are superficial lesions of the mucosa and submucosa and who are healing spontaneously.

Incidence, epidemiology: Peptic ulcer is affecting about 10% of general population, but the true values can’t be known exactly because the endoscopical evidence is not achieved in every case. Peptic ulcer of the duodenum is concerning more the young male, while de ulcer of the stomach is affecting a population of a superior decade of age, belonging to a less wealthy social status.

Etiology and pathogeny: the occurrence of the peptic ulcer is the result of an imbalance between the defending mechanisms of the mucosa and the clorhidropeptic constant aggression.

The defending mechanisms of the mucosa are multiple and complex. A really rapid cellular turn-over offers new, healthy cells in the first row of the mucosa, replacing the old, damaged, unfunctional cells. The mucus secretion produces a continuous film that coates the surface of the mucosa, forming an active barrier against retrodiffusion of the acid. Secretion of the bicarbonate, especially into the duodenum, makes a buffer against clorhidric acid. An adequate blood supply assured by a healthy microcirculation offers the conditions for all this processes to happen.

Although both gastric and duodenal ulcer are comprisedunder the same name, of peptic ulcer, the producing mechanisms are different for each location. Acid secretion was considered for a long time the only factor involved, hence the expression “no acid, no ulcer”, but the clinical studies in the past decades have shown a more complex situation. The most important role in producing gastric ulcer is the impairment of the mucosal defending mechanism. Two are the main ethiological factors involved: the Helicobacter pylori infection and the use of nonsteroidian anti-inflammatory drugs NSAD. Seldom, to these two factors, can be associated acid hypersecretion, caused by gastrin secretory tumors – gastrinoma (which leads to the Zollinger-Elison syndrome). Helicobacter pylori action is complex, but mainly alters the resistance of the mucus coat, which permits the acid to retrodiffuse among the cells, destroying them. More, the presence of the bacteria induces a local inflammatory response, altering the normal consistency of the mucosa. NSAD lower the prostaglandin secretion, irrespective of the way of administration (oral, intravenous, rectal etc.). Prostaglandins have the role of stimulating mucus secretion and decreasing the acid secretion, support the net of vessels that supplies the mucosa. Between 10 and 30 percent of the NSAD users suffer of gastric peptic ulcer. There are others conditions that can act as favorating factors. Amid this, smoking is important, because alters the vascularisation of the mucosa and lowers the prostaglandin secretion. Duodeno-gastric reflux, containing bile, alters the quality of the mucus, the same consequence having the gastric stasis.

In contrast, the duodenal ulcer’s most important cause is the acid hypersecretion. These patients have high values of the Basal Acid Output BAO and Maximal Acid Output MAO. To this it added the rest already mentioned factors, such is the H. Pylori infection and the NSAD use. Some of these patients have certain motility disorder of the stomach, manifested by a rapid evacuation of the gastric content, containing high volumes of acid, into the duodenum, which has a normal or slower motility. This fact put in longer contact de acid hypersecretion with the duodenal mucosa. Smoking remains an important risk factor, being known, beside H. Pylori, the main cause of failure of treatment in duodenal ulcer.

Clinical features. Diagnosis: Pain dominates the entire clinical manifestation and is located either in the epigastrum, either in the hypocondrums, depending on the localisation of the ulcer. The gastric ulcer hurts, classically, in the epigastrum or in the left hypocondrum, of medium intensity, precipitated or aggravated by the food ingestion, made too fast by the patient. Nausea, vomiting and loss of weight could be associated. The duodenal ulcer hurts in the epigastric area, towards the right hypocondrum. The pain is manifested as a “painful hunger”, ameliorated by the food ingestion, especially alkaline, such as milk products, and some of the patients describe a sensation of fullness and nausea. It was described a seasonal exacerbation of pain, during spring and autumn, named “the big periodicity”.

Physical examination in uncomplicated cases is not specific, revealing an epigastric dullness at palpation. The role of clinical examination is more important in complicated cases, like in perforation, for positive and differential diagnosis.

;Regular lab tests are unspecific. For positive diagnostic superior digestive endoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard. Endoscopy allows a direct vision of the lesion and makes biopsy possible. Biopsy is taken from the lesion and from the surrounding area, in order to rule out cancer. A lesion which is believed to be ulcer will not be labeled as an ulcer until the multiple biopsies prove this. In conditions in which the endoscopy is not available, the sole imaging test remains radiology. Historically speaking, radiology with contrast (barium) was the first test that could diagnose gastric and duodenal ulcer, but beared a medium specificity and sensibility. With the use of hidrosoluble contrast and the double contrast technique, these two figures raised to 90%. The traditional radiological image of the ulcer is “the Haudek niche”.

In case of an ulcer, the upmost importance is to detect H. Pylori infection. This is done in real time, on the bioptic specimen, or could be achieved by the respiratory or fecal test.

Classification: By the moment of occurrence, ulcers could be acute, with a diameter of 1cm, fine wedges, and chronic, with a diameter larger than 2 cm and fibrous, infiltrated wedges.

Gastric ulcers were classified by Johnson in five classes, related to ulcer location. Type I is a single ulcer, localised at the gastric angle, Type II associates a gastric to a duodenal ulcer, Type III consists in a single lesion located prepiloric and Type IV are ulcers located high, on the lesser curvature, right under the cardia. Type V is a class added in the last decades, it consist in ulcers caused by the use of NSAD and can be located anywhere on the stomach. This classification has a therapeutical importance, type I and IV are typical gastric ulcers, are not caused by hyperacidity, Type II and III manifest more as a duodenal ulcer, the hyperacidity playing an important role.

Treatment: Uncomplicated cases of peptic ulcer belong to the gastroenterology or internal medicine. The principles that rules the conduit of a case is to lower the acid secretion as much as possible, using agents as proton pump inhibitors IPP, or antagonist of histamine receptors, and the increase of gastro-duodenal mucosal protection, by administrating magnesium and aluminum salts, prostaglandins and, of course, anti H. pylory antibiotic therapy. Surgery is required only in complicated cases, with life-threatening situations or in which there is no response in curability, despite the drug therapy correctly applied.

Complications: There are two acute events that can complicate the natural evolution of an ulcer, which is perforation and, more often, haemorrhage from the ulcer. The chronic evolution of the disease leads to a rare complication – the obstructive emptying gastric outlet.

Perforated peptic ulcer

It is produced by the progression of the erosive lesion through all the layers of the stomach or duodenum wall, including serosa, followed by the outlet of the digestive content into the peritoneum. This phenomenon develops a generalised peritonitis – in typical form, or a localised peritonitis, in atypical forms. Perforation is involving mostly the anterior wall ulcers. The duodenal ulcer offer more cases than the gastric one, because is more frequent, but the general rate of perforation is equal for both, around 10%. Most affected are the second, the third and the fourth decades of life, especially in male.

Depending on the site of the ulcer, the neighboring organs and the peritoneal reaction one divides several variants of perforation:

1. Free perforation – with generalised secondary peritonitis, is the

classical form, frequent.

2. Covered perforation – with a clinical manifestation varying from

the frust form, in which the perforation diameter is small and it is

covered from the beginning by the peritoneal reaction, to the form

with localized peritonitis (peritoneal abscesses).

3. Penetration – represents the progression of erosion towardsand

through the neighboring organs, which are bending to the

gastric/duodenal wall by the aderentia caused by the

scleroinflammatory processes associated. When penetration happens

into a cavitary organ one constitutes a fistula (gastro-colic,

duodeno-colic).

Clinical workout

Ulcer history: could or not be positive, in almost 20% of cases perforation is the first manifestation of the disease. Aggravating factors, such as smoking, NSAD use, aspirin, stress are found in more the half of the patients. Symptoms. Pain:It is the most important symptom in perforation; it is present from the beginning. Pain could follow a certain period of ulcer symptomatology, which suddenly worsens, or it appears brutally, without any announcing signs. First is epigastric localised and could irradiate towards the shoulders, because of the diaphragmatic irritation. Then the pain usually migrates on the right flank, due to the position of the mesocolon, before being generalised. It is aggravated by any movement, the patient breath superficially, tends to be immobile, looking for an antalgic position. After a few hours the pain is losing its strength for a while, then reappears with the same intensity. Vomits are not mandatory, when present, could be associated with haematemesis. In the late stages they become abundant, due to the paralytic ileus. Signs. Shock:Because of the brutal irritation of the peritoneum, vago-vagal reflexes can occur, manifested by a state of shock, with bradicardia, hypotension, pallor, sweating. In the late phases of the natural evolution the shock will be complex, hypovolemic and toxic, due to the bacterian peritonitis. Peritonitic signs: Patients present „the wodden abdomen”, the permanent, involuntary contracture of the abdominal muscles. Patients accuse intense pain when examined, including superficial palpation. The rectal or vaginal examination is very painful (irritation of the Douglas pouch). If localised peritonitis, the abdominal contracture will be replaced by guarding in epigastrum or right iliac fossa, which couldmimicappendicitis. In the late stages abdominal distention appears, in context of ileus and bacterian peritonitis. Respiratory impairment and disparition of the hepatic dullness are result of the gas accumulation and phrenic irritation, but they are not constant.

Laboratory test: Leukocytosis is common and transitory raised levels of serum and urinary amylase are encountered, due to the large peritoneal absorption from the deversated content. Plain abdominal X-Ray is used to pinpoint the pneumoperitoneum, the free gas under the diaphragmappearing as a semilunar shape under the diaphragm, in standing patients, or under the anterior abdominal wall in patients laying. Barium contrast is forbidden, causing a sever peritonitis associated with high rates of mortality, but hidrosoluble agents can be used to evidentiate the outflow of gastro-duodenal content into the peritoneum. Computed tomography is a useful tool to identify pneumoperitoneum in severe cases, in whom plain X-Rays are not conclusive or available. Superior digestive endoscopy is totally contraindicated in these cases, because the gas insufflation will increase the pneumoperitoneum and will accelerate the spill of gastric content; in cases with covered perforation, the gas insufflation could separate the aderentia that block the ulcer.

Positive diagnostic:Usually is simple, based on the patient’s history clinical appearance and the presence of the pneumoperitoneum. About hundred years ago, Mondor established the three cardinal signs of perforated peptic ulcer: acute pain, abdominal rigidity and history of ulcer.

Differential diagnostic: Every disease that evolves with intense pain in the upper abdomen should be taken in discussion: ulcer penetration, acute pancreatitis, acute colecystitis, renal colics, intestinal infarctation. There are several illnesses from the thoracic cage that can mimic perforated peptic ulcer: inferior myocardic infarction, basal pneumonitis, zona zoster.

Treatment

In case of perforating peptic ulcer one must respect the following basic rules:

1. Resting in bed.

2. Installation of a naso-gastric tube and active aspiration of the content.

3. Establishment of intravenous ways – at least two, and administration of

crystalloid solution.

4. Inject IPP iv. If there are no IPP available, choose anti H2.

5. Broad spectrum antibiotics iv.

6. Administration of iv short acting time antalgic (petidine). Those will

ease the patient and will not mask the clinical aspect of eventually

complications.

7. Urgent transport in a surgical emergency unit.

Non-surgical treatment (conservative): Though almost 40% of perforated peptic ulcers are believed to heal spontaneously, the non-surgical treatmentshould be considered always the second choice. Known as Taylor therapy (an American military doctor), this consist in several gestures: nihil per os (nothing by mouth), continuous gastric aspiration, intravenous fluid replacement, iv IPP, iv broad spectrum antibiotherapy and then specific anti H. pylori antibiotics. The antibiotherapy must last two weeks and the acid secretion must be suppressed for four weeks. This method was invented during WW II, for soldiers who suffered a perforation during the battle, till the surgery was available, but it could still be applied in hospitals, if certain rules are followed.

Indications for conservative treatment:

1. When there is absolutely certainty the perforation is blocked and

there are no signs of generalised peritonitis.

2. When the perforation occurs days ago and the status of the patient is

stabile.

3. When, in presence of the two rules above, the patient could be

evaluated clinico-radiological every time needed.

4. When there is no surgical facilities available (ships, oil rigs, isolated

sites) till the patient is removed.

5. Elderly patients with no signs of peritonitis, but with high anesthetic

and surgical risk associated.

Counter-indications for conservative treatment:

1. Positive signs of peritonitis;

2. Contrast spill at radiology;

3. Hemodynamic instability, state of shock;

4. Elderly, but with low operatory risk;

5. Impossibility of follow the course of the patient;

6. Failure of the conservative treatment after 12-24 hours.

Surgery: The surgical intervention stillremains the first choice in perforated peptic ulcer. The surgeon is dealing with the perforation and the peritonitis. There are discussions about using resection as a definitive method in treating a perforated peptic ulcer, usually the surgeon prefer to close the perforation with a patch of great omentum and an abundant peritoneal wash-out. Peptic ulcer haemorrhage

It is responsible for at least 70% of upper digestive haemorrhages and, among ulcer complications, it is the most life-threatening one, with a mortality of 5-10%.

The origin of the bleeding could be old, large ulcers, or new, acute ulcers. The old one are large, fibrous and profound, usually eroding a big vessel outside the gastric wall (i.e. left coronary artery, pyloric artery, gastroduodenalis artery), with a subsequent major haemorrhage, requiring active surgical or endoscopical haemostasis. The new, acute ulcers erode vessels from the mucosa or submucosa, the resulting haemorrhages being less severe, with spontaneous haemostasis in most cases.

Diagnosis and treatment:Upper digestive endoscopy for an ulcer haemorrhage is the first indicated maneuver, being in the same time, diagnostic and therapeutic.The Forrest classification of the bleeding ulcer has practical utility, coding the therapeutical approach depending of the endoscopical aspect.

Forrest classification:

Ia.– in jet arterial bleeding. Usually requires urgent surgical intervention. Occasionally endoscopy can achieve haemostasis;

Ib. – slow, continuous bleeding, venous and capillary in origin: endoscopical haemostasis;

II⑪a. – ceased bleeding, adherent cloth covering the ulcer: intensive peptic ulcer therapy;

IIb⑭. –ceased bleeding, vessel’s stump visible in the crater: high risk of re-bleeding, requires surgery;s

IIc. –ceased bleeding, black crater: standard medical treatment;

III.– ulcer without any signs of bleeding, but with history of haemorrhage: standard medical treatment.

Differential diagnosis is essential for a correct therapeutic approach. Different origins of bleeding must be excluded (epistaxis, faringian tumors, haemoptisia, haemangiomas, vascular abnormalities, aterosclerosis etc.). General conditions could generate digestive haemorrhage: thrombocytopenia, haemophilia, anticoagulant therapy. Into digestive tract, haemorrhage could originate from ruptured oesophagian varices, mucosal erosions, tumors, Mallory- Weiss syndrome.

Therapeutical approach: As previously presented, Forrest’s classification offers a good guide-line for definitive treatment of a bleeding ulcer. Surgery is formal indicated for type Ia, where the amount of bleeding is life threatening and for type IIa, where the surgeon must complete haemostasis already achieved, as soon as possible after the patient stabilisation. For the rest of the cases, the treatment consists of the same gestures as in any gastrointestinal haemorrhage: resuscitation, diagnosis, treatment, re-bleeding prevention.

Surgery has reduced its’ role in treatment of the bleeding ulcers, with the advent of endoscopy, which is able to control most of the cases. Still, indications for surgery remain strong in some situation, in which prognosis of non-surgical treatment is poor.

Clinical features that indicate surgery:

a. Age over 60 years;

b. Long history of ulcer;

c. Frequent relapse on full treatment;

d. Continued melena or haematemesis;

e. More than 4 units of blood transfusion required during resuscitation.

Endoscopic features that indicate surgery:

a. Active bleeding(Forrest Ia);

b. Visible vessel (Forrest IIab);

c. Continued bleeding in spite of correct endoscopic therapy;

d. Relapse after endoscopic treatment;

e. Torrential bleeding that make impossible identification of the lesion .

Gastroduodenal outflow obstruction

This is a chronic complication, evolving after a long history of untreated/ relapsing peptic ulcer. Because this condition is mostly affecting prepiloric and duodenal ulcers, it was inaccurate named pyloric stenosis, but could occur in other anatomical parts of the stomach and the duodenum (i.e. mediogastric stenosis with “hourglass stomach” image at X-Ray).The process of stenosis is due to prolonged history of an ulcer, which induce an inflammatory infiltration around the ulcer, and then fibrotic scarring, modifying the normal anatomy by retraction. A peptic ulcer is considered stenotic when morning gastric resting juice is over 200 ml and a pediatric endoscopic can’t pass through.

After the onset of the fibrotic and stenotic changes, the stomach is compensating by dilatation and hypertrophy of the muscularis. Then failure of compensation occurs and the stomach is dilating and abundant vomiting appears. First phase is called stenic, in which the stomach is fighting against the obstacle. It is featured by scarce symptoms, nothing to reveal the presence of the stenosis. This is followed by the atonic phase, in which the main symptom are profuse vomiting, containing gastric juice, food ingested 1 or 2 days before and is always free from bile. Because of massive vomiting, the patients present also loss if weight, dehydration, constipation and weakness.

Through the unceasing vomitus one loses, also, large amount of fluids, protons (H+ from the acid), chlorine, potassium, natrium. This will figure the umoral-metabolic syndrome of Darrow, characterized by dehydration and “the 3 hypo”: hypokalemia, hyponatremia and hypochloremia. At first the urine will be alkaline, and then acid, due to the efforts of the kidneys to preserve the ions. As a whole, Darrow syndrome is depicted as metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria.

Clinical features: During the stenic phase the patient don’t seems to realise changes in his base symptomatology apart of seldom vomits. When the stomach begins to dilate, the vomiting start to be more copious, ease the patient (after a while the affected person will try to provoke itself). The content of vomitus is free from bile, rich in gastric juice and could include food ingested previous day. At first vomiting is accompanied by nausea, then becomes effortless, explosive, without premonitory signs. In dehydrated and skinny patients, the peristaltic of the stomach could be seen through the tegument (the Kuessmaul sign). If one succusses the abdominal skin of a laying patient, a splashing sound could be heard (the clapotage sign). The late stage of the atone phase is figured by enormous dilatation of the stomach, severe dehydration, complete digestive intolerance to food and water, state of shock.

Diagnosis: Apart of clinical features of peptic disease, the diagnosis of obstruction of the gastric outflow relies on the endoscopic and radiologic aspect. As mentioned, at endoscopy one discovers a dilated stomach, with a chronic ulcer and a stenosis, usually in the pyloric region, tight and insurmountable by a pediatric endoscope. If a barium meal is used, during the stenicphase hyperkinesis of the antrum, with weak duodenal passage is characteristic. Because of the large amount of gastric juice, the barium is seen falling as snowflakes. In the atone phase dilated stomach appears dropped in the pelvic area, looking as a “plate bottom” or “in sink”.

Treatment: Though the surgeons’ aim is to reestablish a normal passage from the stomach into the duodenum, the pyloric stenosis represents a delayed emergency. In the foreground stay all the measures to rebalance the hydration and acid base status.

1. Insert a nasogastric tube for aspiration. This will evacuate the

stomach, cease the vomits, avoid the aspiration into the lungs and

permit to evaluate the hydric losses.

2. Assure at least two venous access point. Saline solution, with a

supplement of ions if necessary, will be administrated, under the

control of ASTRUP parameters.

3. Protein solution (amino acids, albumin) will be required if

hypoproteinemia.

4. If anemia is present, blood and related products are helpful.

The act of surgery can be done only when the patient is well balanced, from the hydric, acid base and protein point of view; otherwise he is exposed to high risk of cardiac arrest, because of ionic unbalance, and anastomotic fistula due to hypoproteinemia. If possible, gastric resection is indicated, this will remove the stenotic area, reduce the volume of the stomach and it has a physiopathologic intent. The continuity of the digestive tract is reestablish by a gastro-duodenal anastomosis (Pean or Billroth I anastomosis), if not possible, a gastro-jejunal anastomosis (Hoffmeister –Finsterer or Billroth II) is preferred. Learning objectives:

  • To know about gastric malignant tumors;
  • To know the importance of early detection of gastric malignant tumors;
  • To know the different therapeutic options and their correlation with the stages of the disease.

History

Apparently, m the first cases of gastric cancer have been mentioned as far back as in antiquity. However, Cruveilhier first described the macroscopic features of a gastric malignant tumor in 1835; later on, Virchow first observed that patients with advanced gastric cancer frequently present with an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node (“Virchow’s node”).

Epidemiology

Although the incidence decreased significantly over the past 75 years in the western countries and the US, gastric cancer still remains the fourth most common cause of cancer-related death:

  • Over 700,000 annual deaths and 990,000 new cases are reported yearly the world over;
  • In the US alone, 22,000 new cases are diagnosed every year, from which 13,000 expire;
  • In Europe, some 140,000 new cases where diagnosed and 107,000 died of GC in 2012.
  • Incidence of gastric cancer is greater in:
  • males compared to females (1.5 to 1);
  • black race;
  • individuals with low economic status;
  • developing countries;
  • Asia (Japan, South Korea, China –70% of all the cases).
  • Risk factors: the most significant (and scientifically proven) risk

factors for developing a malignant gastric tumor are:

  • Helicobacter pylori chronic infection 1- Cigarette smoking; 2-Excessive salts and nitrates intake/salt or smoke preserved food; 3- Diet low on fresh fruits and vegetables; 4-Heredity – hereditary gastric cancers occur in patients with GC positive family history (10-15% of cases; example, the family of Napoleon Bonaparte, emperor of France).
  • HNPCC (hereditary non-polyposic colon cancer syndrome)
  • Lynch syndrome II; these patients have a significantly higher risk for developing a gastric cancer, a colic cancer or both. 5-Gastric diseases predisposing to GC:
  • Giant hypertrophic gastropathy (Menetrier’s disease) – a rare disease, in which the inner laining of the stomach forms huge folds, due to an excessive overgrowth of the mucous membrane;
  • Adenomatous polyps – their surface is covered by mucosa with glands presenting different degrees of atypias; they can degenerate into GC if larger than 2 cm, or/and present high degree atypias;
  • Chronic atrophic gastritis – its incidence is higher in Helicobacter pylori positive cases and presents a significant risk of progression to GC;
  • Remote partial gastrectomy for peptic ulcer (20-30 years) – these patients have a higher risk for GC (infection with Helicobacter pylori is favourized by postgastrectomy diminished acid levels);
  • Intestinal metaplasiais a premalignant lesion, frequently associated with Helicobacter pylori infection and cigarette smoking.

Pathology

A. Histogenesis: Gastric carcinomas arise from the mucosa, in most cases on a previously altered one:

  • The first step in the long process of carcinogenesis is the intestinal metaplasia, during which the chronic inflamed gastric mucosa progressively loses its’ normal appearance, morphing into another type of mucosa, basically foreign to the stomach, an intestinal type.
  • The next step, that of structural degeneration, is the dysplasia of the already altered mucosa; the intensity of the dyspalsic alteration is quantified by three degrees (light, moderate and severe); if the light type of dysplasia does not require surgical treatment, the severe dysplasia is nowadays being considered equal to the notion of “in situ carcinoma” and requires a more aggressive approach (such as endoscopic mucosal excision or a gastric resection).
  • The final step is the progression to invasive carcinoma.

B. Gross appearance:

I. Exterior aspect: Advanced lesions are visible and palpable during

surgical exploration. They appear as firm, infiltrated, sometimes

white/grey colored.

II. Endogastric aspect: can be preoperatively explored endoscopically

(postoperatively, by opening the gastric resected specimen); it may

present, given the state of evolution, as two variants:

1. Early gastric cancer, and

2. Advanced gastric cancer.

1. Early gastric cancer (EGC) – is defined as a local adenocarcinoma, limited to the gastric mucosa or submucosa, notwithstanding the surface of extension, with or without lymph-node metastases. Generally, EGC is rarely occurrent (5-6% in Eastern countries, less than 20% in Western countries). Nevertheless in countries from South-East Asia (Japan, SouthKorea), 50-55% of all gastric cancer cases are detected in this early phase, due to an active

mass screening!

EGC has the best prognosis, with a 5-years survival rate of over 90%!

The diagnosis in this early state of the disease is established only by gastroscopy; based on these findings, the gross endoscopic appearance of EGC has been classified as follows (“The Paris endoscopic classification”)(5):

  • Type 0-I: protrusive, exophytic. May correspond to an actual tumor, rough, protrusive, or to a malignant small polyp.
  • Type 0-II: superficial, non-polypoid, non-excavated, subdivided into three subtypes:
  • Type 0-IIa: slightly elevated (up to 5mm above the surrounding mucosa);
  • Type 0-IIb: flat, discolored mucosa;
  • Type 0-IIc: slightly depressed.
  • Type 0-III: superficial ulceration.

2.Advanced gastric cancer(AGC) – is characterized by the extension of malignant infiltration beyond the submucosa.

Tumors’ gross appearance can vary and is classified in four types, according to the Bormann classification system(4):

  • Type I: protrusive, proliferative
  • Type II: ulcerative, with elevated uneven margins
  • Type III: ulcerative – infiltrating uncertainly contoured tumor, with deep central crater
  • Type IV: extensive infiltrating with important thickening of the gastric wall.

These particular variants are known also as “linitis plastica” or as “gastric schirus”; the gross appearance of the stomach is that of a rigid tube with thick, infiltrated walls (“leather bottle”).

C. Histology:90% of all gastric malignant tumors are adenocarcinomas.

Other histologic varieties are:

  • Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs)

I – Intestinal-type gastric carcinoma of the body or antrum

(non-diffuse, non-proximal)

This is the most common variant. Carcinogenesis follows the

previously described multistep pattern (chronic inflammation –

intestinal metaplasia – dysplasia – invasive carcinoma), and the risk

factors are:

-Helicobacter pylori infection,

  • cigarette smoking,
  • high salt intake,
  • alcohol consumption. II – Gastro-esophageal junction and cardia (proximal) gastric cancer In this variant, infection with Helicobacter pylori seems to have a protective effect (resulted severe atrophic gastritis and aclorhydria, diminishes the risk of gastroesophageal reflux). III – Diffuse type

Here carcinogenesis is triggered by a gene (E-cadherin) mutation. The

not generating a limited, protrusive tumor, but an extended thickening of

the entire stomach, which becomes a rigid tube.

  • tends to appear in younger patients,

Diagnosis of gastric cancer

A.Clinical features: What characterizes gastric cancer (and most of the digestive tract tumors) is that there are no specific clinical signs or symptoms. Moreover, in the early phases, there might be no symptom at all. Progressively, paralleling the growth of the tumor, non-specific symptoms may occur:

  • epigastric discomfort
  • flatulence
  • postprandial meteorism
  • early satiation
  • malaise.

The so-called “alarm symptoms”usually occur in more advanced stages of GC:

  • dysphagia
  • upper digestive tract hemorrhage
  • fatigue
  • anemia
  • weight loss
  • selective anorexia (for meat, bread)
  • epigastric palpable tumor.
  • Juxtaorificially situated tumors (eso-gastric junction or pyloric) can manifest

somewhat sooner due to early alteration of local motility/functionality (end-esophagus, pylorus), resulting in early dysphagia or gastroesophageal reflux, heartburn, and regurgitation, in tumors located at the esophagogastric junction.

  • In distal antro-pyloric-located, stenotic tumors, in time, late gastric emptying (sensation of fullness) progressively evolves in the classic “malignant pyloric stenosis” or “malignant gastric outlet obstruction”, with consequently voluminous food vomiting, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, weight loss, emaciation and finally, if untreated, cachexia (loss of skeletal muscle mass).
  • Anemic syndrome – digestive hemorrhaging is “occult” to begin with,

clinically undetectable (neither in vomit nor in stool), but persistent, leading in time to chronic iron deficiency anemia (a common finding in digestive tract malignant tumors!). As a result, headache, weakness or fatigue, decreased efficiency at work and pallor occur.

  • Of overwhelming importance is the concept of “oncologic vigilance”,as any time such patients are found, it is necessary to subject their feces to a “Haemocult” test. This test may detect the presence of minimal quantities of blood within the stool sample. Once positivated, this test will invite an endoscopic evaluation of the digestive tract. Let us not forget thusly, that in this early stage, the patient is neither cachectic, nor in experiencing any pain and may not have any kind of symptom, excepting, maybe, a slight weakness, and/or a moderate pallor (the chance of early diagnosis!).
  • At the opposite end of hemorrhage severity scale, dramatic, acute, massive episodes ofgastric hemorrhages, although rare, may occur (example – erosion of splenic artery with life-threatening massive intragastric hemorrhage, by a posterior gastric tumor, invading the pancreas).
  • Moderate upper digestive hemorrhaging are not rare; sometimes these hemorrhagic episodes might be the initial manifestation (revealing complication); the gastroscopy performed at presentation will establish the diagnosis. They can beexteriorized through: * hematemesis (fresh blood – meaning active hemorrhage, or digested, “coffee-dregs”-like blood – meaning a previous hemorrhagic episode, stopped at the moment of examination); * melenic stools (soft, black, tarry feces).
  • Anorexia (frequently selective, for meat and bread), combined with an

excessivecatabolism of the muscles, will lead to progressive weigh loss(there are cases with unexplained, unintentioned weigh loss in spite of initial normal appetite!) and finally to cachexia (from Greek kakos=bad; heksis=condition). The result is the so-called anorexia-cachexiasyndrome, with severe a decrease of performance status. It occurs in the majority of advanced gastrointestinal cancers and is one of the contributing factors to life shortening of the patients.(In these cases, serum albumin level most accurately reflects patient’s nutritional status).

  • In very advanced stages, with disseminated disease, the following signs and

symptoms may occur (always indicating iresectability!):

  • Jaundice (intrahepatic – due to multiple liver metastases;extrahepatic – due to external compression of CBD by voluminous metastatic lymph nodes, or even to CBD direct invasion by the gastric tumor).
  • Increase in abdominal volume, due to peritoneal effusion (ascitis) – speaks for peritoneal carcinomatosis.
  • Irregular, large liver signifies the presence of large metastases.
  • Virchow’s node – left large supraclavicular or laterocervical lymph nodes.
  • Sister Mary Joseph’s node – umbilical metastatic nodule.
  • Blumer’s shelf – large peritoneal/intestinal metastasis, “fallen” deep into the Douglas’ pouch, thus detected during the rectal examination.
  • Kruckenberg tumors – “paradoxical”ovarian metastases of the gastric tumor, detectable as well at vaginal examination.
  • Intense, persisting epigastric pain with dorsal irradiation – might signify posterior invasion of the pancreas and of the celiac plexuses.

B. Paraclinical diagnosis

1.Gastroscopy: is nowadays the main examination. Any patient presenting with dyspepsia, associated with one or more of the alarm signs, or with positive family history of GC, should be promptly explored endoscopically, thus obtaining a direct internal view of the stomach; the encountered aspect may vary, but always remains suggestive to an experienced endoscopist (red, irregular tumor or ulceration, with grey/necrotic areas, quick to bleed when touched – see pathology). Alongside there is the possibility of simultaneous biopsy of the suspected lesion (the only way to ascertain preoperative diagnosis!).

Nevertheless we do emphasize the fact that a negative biopsy does never exclude the existence of a cancer! In such cases, with grossly suspect lesions and negative biopsies, close follow up, with repeated gastroscopies and biopsies is mandatory. For example, a gastric ulcerative cancer can be erroneously considered as benign (based on the initial negative biopsies). Moreover, it may even heal temporary under medical treatment. Hence, repeated endoscopic and bioptic reevaluations are needed, as a misdiagnosed cancer might lie behind the apparently benign ulceration. Brushing cytology examination – gentle brushing of the lesion – may detect malignant cells where biopsies failed to confirm its’ malignant nature!

Very small, superficial lesions (EGC) can be nowadays accurately diagnosed using modern endoscopic techniques:

(1) Magnifying endoscopy

(2) Narrow band imaging

(3) Chromoendoscopy (with indigo carmine used as staining agent).

2. Radiology:with the increasing accessibility of endoscopic examinations, the radiological exploration of the stomach has lost much of its importance. However it has the advantage of being largely accessible, cheap, and generates no complications.

  • Barium examination, with the two techniques, “double contrast” or

“thin layer”, may still detect small gastric lesions, sometimes even an early gastric cancer.

-The radiological signs are: segmental rigidity of the infiltrated area of the gastric wall; the most relevant one is the lacunar image, representing a “filling deficiency”, corresponding to a tumor jutting out into the gastric lumen.

  • Percutaneous abdominal ultrasound examination –is cheap,

noninvasive, largely accessible; it therefore is used as a first intention exploration, giving important orientating data concerning lymph node involvement (N-stage) and the presence of liver secondaries (M-stage). In cases with suspect hepatic lesions, contrast enhanced ultrasonography more accurately establishes their benign or malignant nature.

  • Endoscopic ultrasound examination – consists of an ultrasound

examination from within the stomach, by endoscopically applying the transducer directly to the lesion, without any interposition. It is the most accurate technique in terms of local extension of a gastric tumor (layer by layer infiltration of the gastric wall, or adjacent organs)(T-stage).

  • Computed Tomography Scanning of the abdominal cavity and pelvis,

with i.v. contrast, offers more accurate data for evaluation of the local extension of the tumor (T-stage), local and regional lymph node involvement (N-stage) and metastatic dissemination (M-stage).

  • Magnetic Resonance Imaging – is selectively used in gastric cancer

staging process; it is more expensive as compared to CT scanning and gives similar information, yet it is superior to the latter in some cases (i.e., in suspect small hepatic lesions detected by CT, MRI in the arterial phase, may define more accurately their presence and nature).

  • Positron Emission Tomography – is also selectively used; the main

benefit of the technique resides in the accurate detection of small and very small distant matastases (i.e. bones, cerebral, lungs).

3. Staging Laparoscopy (SL) – is not systematically used in the staging of gastric cancers; still, in well selected cases, it may ascertain the presence of very small peritoneal or hepatic capsular metastases (peritoneal carcinomatosis), lesions only suspected but not detected with certainty by the aforementioned imaging techniques. Some do advocate peritoneal cytology; well, if there are no macroscopic peritoneal seeds, in patients with small ascites, positive cytology does not preclude the gastric resection; in these cases, however, the procedure must be considered as a palliative one as positive peritoneal cytology is classified as M1, disseminated disease – stage IV! (In patients with macroscopic, yet millimetric multiple peritoneal seeds, gastric resection does not offer survival benefit anymore, as such a late stage IV case has already a very limited life expectancy. Thus in these cases, SL helps avoiding an unnecessary laparotomy.

4. Tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9, CA72-4, CA50) – are lacking satisfactory specificity. These values increase mostly in the advanced stages. They play a role however in appreciating the accuracy of surgical resection (should drop postoperatively to normal values in case of a radical R0 resection); they may rise the suspicion of metastases or local recurrence during postoperative follow-up (case in which these values increase anew, months before imaging detection).

We do emphasize that none of the aforementioned diagnostic techniques is complete in terms of accurate staging. Only their wise combination/selection by the clinician will uncover all the necessary details for a complete evaluation of the case.

Accurate preoperative staging is crucial,as to each individual case with its’ specific stage corresponds a specific therapeutic protocol!

Prognosis of gastric carcinoma

  • Generally, the prognosis of gastric cancer is dismal. Untreated, it can lead to demise within 12-18 months since first detection.
  • With proper treatment –gastric R0 resection – (+/-oncological treatment, depending on stage), approximately 20% of all cases survive for 5 years.
  • EGC has, when treated, by far a better prognosis, with a survival rate at 5 years of over 90% (whence the importance of early diagnosis!)
  • GC located on the gastric body and fundus are frequently found late, thus curative treatment is not possible in many cases (lacking symptoms until advanced stages); on the contrary, the ones found on the extremities of the stomach (oesophago-gastric junction, pylorus), present signs earlier. Distal (antro-pyloric) tumors have the highest respectability rates and the best prognosis.

Complications of gastric cancer

Excepting generalization/dissemination/metastasizing – which is in fact the last stage in the natural evolution of the disease – the complications of GC are similar with those of gastric peptic ulcer: haemorrhage, stenosis, perforation, and invasion of neighboring viscera.

Treatment of gastric adenocarcinoma

  • - Theonly chance for cure in gastric adenocarcinomas is radical, complete (R0), resection.
  • - Both endoscopic and surgical approaches are available, depending on the stage of the disease.
  • - The type and extent of resection is selected using endoscopic and pathologic criteria(11-Tomoyuki) resulted from evaluation of both the T-category (local extension of the tumor) and the N-category (regional lymph nodes).

I -Endoscopic (nonsurgical) resections:

  • Minimally invasiveness of this nonsurgical procedures offer the advantage of completely preserving the morphologic and functional integrity of the abdominal wall and the stomach!
  • Are indicated only: * in intestinal type lesions (not in diffuse type), confined to the superficial layers of the gastric wall (mucosa/submucosa: Tis, T1a, T1b); * without lymph node metastases (N0).
  • Eradication of Helicobacter pylori is mandatory in order to prevent a metachronous gastric carcinoma after the excision.

Statistically, the frequency of positive lymph nodes in intramucosal EGCs is low (0.4-3%).In submucosal carcinomas however, up to 20% of cases have lymph node metastases. As no present imagistic technique is able to perfectly accurate sort these cases out, selection criteria of cases with the lowest probability of having positive lymph nodes have been established based on pathological studies, by the JGCA (Japan Gastric Cancer Association) (15), as follows:

  • Endoscopic Mucosal Resection(EMR): is indicated only in EGC cases

confined to the mucosa, with no positive lymph nodes detected during the preoperative evaluation.The following criteria are in use:

* mucosal–well differentiated, elevated, ≤ 20mm;

* well differentiated, depressed, < 10mm, no ulcer;

* The draw-back of this procedure is that the surface of the excisable

lesion is small. Larger lesions cannot always be totally resected(risk

of recurrence – R1 resection!).

  • Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection (ESD): allows for a larger and

deeper, en block resection, following the plan between the submucosa and the muscular layer; indicated according to the following criteria:

* mucosal carcinoma – well differentiated, > 20mm, no ulcer;well

differentiated, ≤ 30mm, with ulcer;

* submucosal carcinoma – well differentiated, ≤ 30mm.

Still, in some cases, the vertical margins of the resected specimen are not free from cancer cells,and the degree of wall infiltration is not always precise. Moreover, there are some gastric areas where lesions are difficult accessible with both the aforementioned techniques (corpus curvature, fundus). Thus, as a solution for both the aforementioned draw-backs, a new technique is evolving:

  • Endoscopic Full Thickness Resection (EFTR):uses a special device

able to resect the small tumor together with all the layers (mucosa, submucosa, muscular layer and serosa – “full thickness”) around the tumor; the resulted gastric wall defect is immediately closed with endoscopic clips.

II - Surgical treatment of gastric cancer

R0, radical, curative resection is the main goal of surgery for gastric malignant tumors; no remnant malignant cells are left in the operating field. In order to achieve this purpose several surgical procedures have been developed for visceral R0 resection (gastrectomies) and for lymph node R0 clearance (lymphadanactomy). Regarding the radicality:

  • the proximal limit of gastric resection must be at least 5-6 cm above the

cranial macroscopic limit of the tumor.

  • lymph node stations to be removed by the D2 lymphadenectomy are

the following: No 1. right paracardial lymph nodes (LN) No 7. LN along the left gastric artery No 2. left paracardial LN No 8. LN along the common hepatic artery No 3. LN along the lesser curvature No 9. LN along the celiac artery No 4. LN along the gastroepiploic vessels No 10. splenic hilum LN No 5. suprapyloric LN No 11. LN along the splenic artery No 6. subpyloric LN No 12. LN in the hepato-duodenal ligament

Extension of gastrectomydepends on where the tumor is located:

  • Wedge resection – may be used in well selected early submucosal

gastric carcinomas this procedure is appropriate for gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs).

  • Subtotal gastrectomy –is indicated in distal (antropyloric) gastric

carcinomas. Resection includes the duodenum (sectioned 3cm distal from the pylorus), pylorus and the distal 3/4 or 4/5 of the stomach.

  • Total gastrectomy – is indicated in tumors located at the gastric corpus

and fundus. The distal resection limit is similar; the proximal one includes 3-5cm of the distal esophagus, thus the entire stomach is resected.

Both in subtotal and total gastrectomies, the large and small omentum remain attached to the gastric specimen – omentectomy(fig.14). The reason why the large omentum must be included in resection is that doing so, lymph node group 4 (around the gastroepiploic vessels) remains attached to the gastric specimen and thus, resected.

However, resection of the stomach and omentum alone provides a radical R0 resection just for the tumor itself, but not with respect of the lymph nodes’ clearance, as gastric resection associated with the omentectomy alone will allow for removing just the perigastric lymph node stations (stations1, 3, 4, 5, and 6).

Extension of lymphadenectomy:After removing the specimen from the operating field, only an incomplete lymphadenctomy was carried out. Thus, the next step is to complete the lymph node clearance; this goal is obtained only by additionally remove the regional lymph node stations 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12in order to accomplish a D2 lymphadenectomy!

Reconstruction:

  • After subtotal gastrectomy, the continuity of the digestive tract is

accomplished by suturing the gastric stump to:

1. duodenal stump (termino-terminal gastro-duodenostomy –Bilroth I

operation);

2. the first jejunal loop (termino-lateral gastro-jejunostomy – Bilroth

II operation);

3. Roux-en-Y jejunal loop (termino-lateralRoux-enY

gastro-jejunostomy).

  • After total gastrectomy – the duodenal stump is closed (mechanical or

by manual suture); the continuity of the digestive tract can be reestablished by numerous techniques, but the most frequently used are:

1. Roux-en Y termino-lateral eso-jejunostomy.

2. Bilroth II with Braun anastomosis– in cases in which, due to

anatomical or vascular particularities, the Roux loop cannot be

prepared, the Bilroth II with Braun anastomosis (i.e., supplementary

latero-lateral jejuno-jejunal anastomosis, distal to the initial

eso-jejunostomy)represents a viable technical alternative.

Laparoscopicsurgery for gastric tumors

All surgical procedures addressed to gastric tumors have nowadays a laparoscopic alternative (in cases without local extension). It is actually the interpretation of the same “symphony” with different instruments.

The advantages of laparoscopic approaches are well established now, in terms of shorter hospital stay, better postoperative comfort, earlier postoperative mobilization, less pain, earlier bowel movements, improved cosmetic.

Laparoscopic gastric resections are presently on a regular base indicated in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs), where, in most of the cases (with low malignancy) gastric security margins of resection are limited (2cm) and lymph nodes involvement is exceptional (no lymphadenectomy needed).

In gastric carcinomas, the radicality of the abovementioned surgical procedures, both in terms of clear visceral resection margins and completeness of lymphadenectomy are nowadays similar to the classic open approach. The long time survival rates are similar as well.

In cases of endoscopically resected early gastric cancers in which a suspicion of concomitant lymph nodes’ involvement persists, laparoscopic lymphadenectomy may be associated.

Thus nowadays global experience with laparoscopic gastric cancer surgery is constantly growing, tending to become the gold standard in the future.

Palliation for advanced gastric cancer

  • Distal non-resectable gastric tumors generating gastric outlet obstruction

will benefit of endoscopic stenting in order to alleviate the obstruction; yet in most of the cases, alaparoscopic or classic/open gastro-enterostomy is necessary to by-pass the obstructive tumor.

  • In very advanced cases, with multiple liver metastases or peritoneal

carcinomatosis, gastric resection is no more indicated. However, bleedings that cannot be controlled by endoscopy mayrequire emergencygastric resections, yet only for haemostatic, not for oncologic reasons. Gastric resections in these cases are exceptional, salvage procedures; they not only do not improve patients’ long time survival, but can generate high morbidity and mortality rates.
